armenian-church-dhaka.desc: Armanitola takes its name from the Armenian traders who settled in Dhaka in the Mughal era. Their church, completed in 1781, stands in a walled compound with old gravestones inscribed in Armenian and English. The whitewashed building and bell tower feel far removed from the busy lanes outside. A caretaker usually opens the gate for respectful visitors.
blocks: How to get there
Walk from Star Mosque in Armanitola; the church is a few lanes away.
Good to know
Knock at the gate and ask politely; a small donation is appreciated.

ahsan-manzil.desc: Ahsan Manzil was the seat of the Nawab family of Dhaka and was rebuilt in its present form after a tornado in 1888. The pink, domed building looks over the Buriganga, and a grand staircase climbs from the front lawn to the first floor. Today it is a national museum with restored rooms, furniture, portraits and displays on the city's 19th-century history. Pair it with a boat ride from the nearby ghats to see the palace from the water.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw from Sadarghat or Islampur Road in Old Dhaka; it sits on Kumartoli, close to the river.
Good to know
Usually closed Thursdays. Photography is not allowed inside the galleries.

glance: Stalls around Chawkbazar Shahi Mosque in Old Dhaka, during Ramadan only
winter (Dec–Jan), spring (Feb–Mar), summer (Apr–May), monsoon (Jun–Jul), autumn (Aug–Sep) and late autumn (Oct–Nov)
chawkbazar-iftar-bazar.desc: Every Ramadan afternoon the lanes around Chawkbazar Shahi Mosque fill with makeshift stalls selling iftar, a custom locals trace back to the British period. The best-known dish is boro baper polay khay, a heavy mix of chickpeas, minced meat, brain, egg, chira, spices and ghee tossed together in a huge pan. Stalls also sell kebabs, roast meats and big coils of shahi jilapi. Many sellers are the second or third generation of their family at the same spot.
blocks: Good to know
Only runs in Ramadan. Arrive by 3–4 pm; it gets very crowded close to iftar time.

jatiya-sangsad-bhaban.desc: The Parliament House at Sher-e-Bangla Nagar was designed by the American architect Louis Kahn and is counted among the great buildings of the 20th century. Huge circles, triangles and slits are cut into its concrete walls, and the whole complex seems to float on the water that surrounds it. The building itself is closed to casual visitors, but the lawns, the lake edge and Manik Mia Avenue in front are open, and in the late afternoon Dhaka families come here to walk. The sunset light on the concrete is the reason most photographers come.
blocks: How to get there
Bus, CNG or rickshaw to Farmgate, Manik Mia Avenue or Asad Gate; the complex sits between them.
Good to know
Go in the late afternoon for the light. Photography of the building from the public roads and lawns is fine; follow guards' instructions near the gates.

national-martyrs-memorial-savar.desc: The National Martyrs' Memorial at Savar honours the people killed in the 1971 Liberation War. Designed by Syed Mainul Hossain, it is built of seven triangular planes that rise steeply to a single peak, and it stands at the end of a long walkway past lawns, pools and mass graves. On 26 March and 16 December huge crowds come to lay flowers. On ordinary days it is calm and green, and a good half-day trip from Dhaka.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus from Gabtoli toward Savar or Nabinagar and get off at the Smriti Soudho gate on the Dhaka–Aricha highway (about 1–1.5 hours from central Dhaka).
Good to know
Avoid the national days if you dislike crowds. Treat the mass-grave area with respect.

glance: Kebab shops around Geneva Camp, near Mohammadpur Government High School, Mohammadpur
winter (Dec–Jan), spring (Feb–Mar), summer (Apr–May), monsoon (Jun–Jul), autumn (Aug–Sep) and late autumn (Oct–Nov)
geneva-camp-kabab-chaap.desc: The Urdu-speaking community of Geneva Camp in Mohammadpur has made this corner one of Dhaka's best-known kebab streets. Once the sun sets, small shops along the camp's edge fire up their grills for flattened beef chaap, kidney (gurda) chaap, brain fry and khiri kebab, eaten with soft paratha or naan. Mustakim's, which began as a stall outside Mohammadpur Government High School, is the best-known name, and several other kebab shops sit in the same row. The lanes inside the camp also sell Bihari sweets and late-night paan.
blocks: Good to know
Stalls open at dusk; in Ramadan they sell iftar boxes from the afternoon.

dhakeshwari-temple.desc: Dhakeshwari means 'goddess of Dhaka', and tradition holds that the city is named after her. The temple complex in old Dhaka is state-owned and is the country's national temple. It holds several shrines, including a row of four Shiva temples, around a courtyard and pond. During Durga Puja and Janmashtami the grounds fill with worshippers and visitors of every faith.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw from Azimpur, Lalbagh or Palashi; it is off Dhakeshwari Road, close to Lalbagh Fort.
Good to know
Take off your shoes before the shrines and dress modestly. Combine it with Lalbagh Fort, which is a short rickshaw ride away.

star-mosque-dhaka.desc: Tara Masjid was built in the early 19th century and later redecorated with chinitikri, a mosaic of broken porcelain and glass. Blue stars cover the domes and walls, while the inside is patterned with floral motifs and tiles, some of them imported. It is still a working mosque, so it is quiet and modest rather than a showpiece. A visit takes less than an hour and fits easily into a walk through Armanitola.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw to Armanitola in Old Dhaka, a few minutes from Ahsan Manzil.
Good to know
Dress modestly and avoid prayer times; women should cover their heads.

mangal-shobhajatra.desc: On 14 April, Bangla New Year, Dhaka wakes early for Pohela Boishakh. The Faculty of Fine Arts of Dhaka University (Charukola) leads a parade of huge papier-mache animals, masks and folk figures, a tradition inscribed by UNESCO in 2016. Elsewhere, Chhayanaut's dawn concert under the banyan tree at Ramna Park welcomes the year with songs. People wear red and white, eat panta-ilish and fill the streets around Shahbag.
blocks: Good to know
Arrive at dawn, expect road closures, and carry water.

glance: Nazira Bazar, Bangshal and Chankharpul in Old Dhaka
winter (Dec–Jan), spring (Feb–Mar), summer (Apr–May), monsoon (Jun–Jul), autumn (Aug–Sep) and late autumn (Oct–Nov)
dhaka-old-town-biryani.desc: Old Dhaka is the heartland of Bangladeshi biryani, from mutton kacchi cooked with raw marinated meat and potato to the mustard-oil scented pakki style. Haji Biryani in Nazira Bazar has served its goat biryani since 1939 and sells out by afternoon. Other shops around Nazira Bazar, Bangshal and Chankharpul serve kacchi, tehari and morog polao. Eat it with borhani, a tangy spiced yoghurt drink.
blocks: Good to know
Go at lunchtime; popular shops run out early.

glance: Roughly 20–60 BDT a plate at street carts
Street carts on Bailey Road, around TSC at Dhaka University, Dhanmondi Lake and Shantinagar
winter (Dec–Jan), spring (Feb–Mar), summer (Apr–May), monsoon (Jun–Jul), autumn (Aug–Sep) and late autumn (Oct–Nov)
dhaka-fuchka-chotpoti.desc: Fuchka are small hollow crisp shells, cracked open and stuffed with spiced mashed dried peas, potato, egg and onion, then eaten in one bite with sour tamarind water. Chotpoti uses the same pea filling served warm in a bowl, topped with egg, chilli and tamarind. Every Dhaka neighbourhood has its carts, but Bailey Road, the TSC area at Dhaka University, Dhanmondi Lake and Shantinagar are long-time favourites. A plate is cheap and evenings are the busiest time.
blocks: Good to know
Pick a busy cart; high turnover means fresher food.

bara-katra.desc: Bara Katra was built between 1644 and 1646 by Mir Abul Qasim, diwan of the Mughal prince Shah Shuja, as a grand inn around a courtyard. The southern wing once faced the Buriganga with a three-storey gateway and octagonal towers at each end. Less than half of it survives, and owners and new buildings have eaten into the rest; part was knocked down in 2022. What remains is the arched gate with a madrasa and shops pressing in on it. It is a hidden piece of old Dhaka that most people walk past without noticing.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw from Lalbagh, Chawkbazar or Sadarghat; it sits just south of Chawkbazar towards the river.
Good to know
Combine it with Lalbagh Fort, Hussaini Dalan and Chawkbazar in one old Dhaka walk. The building is in private and madrasa use, so look from outside and ask before photographing inside.

baldha-garden.desc: Baldha Garden was laid out in Wari by a zamindar of Baldha, Narendra Narayan Roy Chowdhury, and is one of the oldest botanical gardens in the country. Its few acres hold hundreds of plant species, including rare water lilies, orchids, cacti and old trees, many brought from abroad. It is now run as a unit of the National Botanical Garden. Few Dhaka visitors know it is there, which is exactly its charm.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw from Gulistan, Motijheel or Wari to the garden gate in Wari.
Good to know
Go in the morning when it is cooler and quiet. Pair it with Rose Garden Palace a few minutes away.

glance: Small ticket for Bangladeshis; higher ticket for foreigners
bangladesh-national-museum.desc: Founded in 1913 as the Dhaka Museum, the National Museum at Shahbag is the best single place to get a feel for Bangladesh's past. Its floors cover stone and bronze sculpture, coins, folk art, textiles, natural history and the 1971 Liberation War. The collection is large, so pick a few galleries rather than trying to see everything. It is a good rainy-day or midday stop.
blocks: How to get there
Bus, CNG or rickshaw to Shahbag; the museum is on the main road next to the Shahbag intersection.
Good to know
The museum is closed on Thursdays (check before going). Bags may have to be left at the counter.

glance: Cheap, sold by the piece or by the kg
Bakeries around Lalbagh, Chawkbazar and Nazira Bazar
winter (Dec–Jan), spring (Feb–Mar), summer (Apr–May), monsoon (Jun–Jul), autumn (Aug–Sep) and late autumn (Oct–Nov)
dhaka-bakarkhani.desc: Bakarkhani is a thick, layered flatbread baked against the walls of a tandoor until it turns crisp and slightly salty or sweet. It has been tied to Old Dhaka for centuries and is still made by hand in tiny bakeries along Lalbagh and Chawkbazar lanes. Locals dunk it in milk tea or eat it with kebab and halua. Watching the bakers slap dough into the oven is half the pleasure.

glance: Beauty Lacchi and Faluda, 30/1 Johnson Road, Old Dhaka (a branch also runs at Nazira Bazar)
winter (Dec–Jan), spring (Feb–Mar), summer (Apr–May), monsoon (Jun–Jul), autumn (Aug–Sep) and late autumn (Oct–Nov)
beauty-lassi-falooda.desc: Beauty Lacchi and Faluda opened on Johnson Road in Old Dhaka in 1922, started by Abdul Aziz, who had sold lemonade and lassi from a street stall before that. His grandsons run it now and say they still follow the old method: yoghurt, sugar and ice churned into a thick lassi, sweet or salted. The lemon sherbet is just as famous, and falooda joined the menu in 2000. It is a short stop between Sadarghat, Ahsan Manzil and the Star Mosque.

glance: winter (Dec–Jan), spring (Feb–Mar), summer (Apr–May), monsoon (Jun–Jul), autumn (Aug–Sep) and late autumn (Oct–Nov)
liberation-war-museum-dhaka.desc: The Liberation War Museum was started by a group of private trustees who asked ordinary people to donate money, letters, weapons and belongings from the 1971 war. Its collection has grown to more than 21,000 items. In 2017 it moved from a cramped old house in Segunbagicha to a purpose-built building in Agargaon, with far more gallery space. The galleries walk you from the Language Movement through the events of 1971 to independence, and some displays are hard to look at. Give it a quiet couple of hours.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus, CNG or ride-share to Agargaon; the museum is on the road between Agargaon and Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, near the metro rail's Agargaon station.
Good to know
Check the opening days before you go. Some galleries show graphic images of the war, so prepare children beforehand. Bags may need to be left at the counter.

rose-garden-palace.desc: Rose Garden Palace was built in the late 19th century by the Hindu zamindar Hrishikesh Das, who was famous for his rose garden. The pale classical mansion with its columns, fountain and statues later passed to another zamindar family. In June 1949 the Awami League was formed here, so it also has a place in political history. Film-makers have long used it as a set, and it is now in government hands.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw from Motijheel, Wari or Gulistan to K.M. Das Lane in Tikatuli.
Good to know
Access to the grounds can be limited, so check locally before you go. Combine it with Baldha Garden nearby.

lalbagh-fort.desc: Work on Lalbagh Fort began in 1678 under the Mughal prince Muhammad Azam and was continued by Shaista Khan, but it was never completed. Inside the walls are three main buildings: a three-domed mosque, the audience hall with its hammam, and the tomb of Pari Bibi, Shaista Khan's daughter. Gardens and old water channels connect them, and the red-brick gateways make good photographs in late-afternoon light. It is one of the few places in Old Dhaka where you can sit on grass and hear birds.
blocks: How to get there
Take a rickshaw or CNG to Lalbagh in Old Dhaka; from Azimpur it is a short rickshaw ride.
Good to know
Closed on Sundays and has shortened hours on Monday. Come in the afternoon and walk on to Dhakeshwari Temple nearby.

glance: Small terminal ticket; nouka rides are negotiated
sadarghat-buriganga.desc: Sadarghat is the main river terminal of Dhaka, with large launches leaving each evening for Barishal, Bhola and other southern towns. Small wooden nouka shuttle passengers across the Buriganga all day, and hiring one for half an hour is the best way to watch the city's working river life. You will see dockyards, cargo boats and the facade of Ahsan Manzil from the water. It is crowded and noisy, which is exactly the point.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw or CNG to Sadarghat in Old Dhaka.
Good to know
Agree the boat fare before boarding, keep valuables close, and go early morning or late afternoon.

shakrain-kite-festival.desc: Shakrain falls on Poush Sankranti, the last day of the Bangla month of Poush, usually around 14–15 January. From morning, families in Shankhari Bazar, Sutrapur, Gendaria and nearby neighbourhoods fly kites from their rooftops and try to cut each other's strings. In the evening there is music, fireworks and young men blowing fire. It is a neighbourhood festival rather than an official event, so the best way in is to know someone with a rooftop.
blocks: Good to know
Join a rooftop gathering through a local contact or guesthouse; watch for falling kite strings in the lanes.

hussaini-dalan.desc: Hussaini Dalan was first built in the 17th century, when Prince Shah Shuja governed Bengal, as a house of mourning for Imam Hussain. The present building is largely an 1823 rebuild, with a flat roof added by the Dhaka Nawabs after the 1897 earthquake, so Mughal and colonial styles sit side by side. A long white hall stands on a raised platform, and on its south side a deep water tank reflects the verandah. In the first ten days of Muharram it fills with majlis gatherings, and the Ashura procession sets out from here.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw from Chankharpul, Bakshibazar or Lalbagh; it is on Hussaini Dalan Road close to Dhaka Medical College.
Good to know
Dress modestly and take off your shoes where asked. Around Ashura the area is very crowded and security is tight, so go on a quieter day if you only want to see the building.
